Mexican Revolution. A prolonged civil conflict and social upheaval from nineteen ten to nineteen twenty that transformed Mexico's political and economic structure. Sparked by resentment of Porfirio Díaz's authoritarian thirty-year rule and the concentration of land in the hands of elites and foreign corporations, the Revolution began as a movement for political reform and evolved into a struggle for agrarian justice, indigenous rights, and national sovereignty. Though the Revolution itself ended around nineteen twenty, its institutional aftermath—a one-party state, land redistribution, and anti-clerical nationalism—defined Mexico for the rest of the twentieth century and made it Latin America's first major social revolution.

Decades of rule by Porfirio Díaz from eighteen seventy-six to nineteen eleven brought economic modernization but massive inequality. Peasants were landless. Foreign corporations controlled mines and oil. Political opposition was suppressed. Francisco Madero, a reformist who called for Tierra y Libertad, Land and Liberty, ran against Díaz in nineteen ten. When Díaz fraudulently reelected himself, Madero's call to arms sparked the Revolution.

Early phases saw Emilio Zapata lead southern peasants demanding land reform, and Pancho Villa command northern armies. Díaz was forced to resign and Madero became president from nineteen eleven to nineteen thirteen. Victoriano Huerta, a conservative general, overthrew Madero in nineteen thirteen and reinstated authoritarian rule, triggering a renewed uprising by Zapata, Villa, and other factions. The Revolution fragmented into multiple armies pursuing different goals: agrarian reform, political democracy, indigenous autonomy, and national sovereignty from foreign especially United States intervention. Battles devastated the countryside. Armies conscripted peasants. Cities changed hands repeatedly. An estimated one million people died in violence, disease, and famine.

The Constitution of nineteen seventeen, drafted by revolutionary delegates, incorporated radical provisions: ejido land collective ownership, limits on foreign landownership, restrictions on the Catholic Church, and strong executive power. Emilio Zapata continued guerrilla warfare in southern Mexico until his assassination in nineteen nineteen, fighting for agrarian reform to be implemented. Pancho Villa surrendered in nineteen twenty. The Revolution's military phase ended by nineteen twenty, though banditry and sporadic uprisings continued. The victors consolidated power into the Institutional Revolutionary Party, which would dominate Mexico for seventy-one years.

Land was redistributed to peasant communities as ejidos. The Church's political power was curtailed. Indigenous communities gained nominal recognition, though often exploited in practice. The Revolution made Mexico the first Latin American nation to implement large-scale land reform and assert sovereignty over natural resources. It inspired later revolutions, notably in Cuba. The Revolution's artistic legacy—muralism by Diego Rivera, David Alfaro Siqueiros, and others—became the twentieth century's most recognizable artistic form celebrating indigenous culture and revolutionary ideals. The Mexican Revolution was Latin America's first major social upheaval, preceding Cuba's by over forty years. Unlike the French or Russian revolutions, it was less ideologically coherent. It blended agrarian reform, indigenous nationalism, anti-clericalism, and anti-imperialism into a distinctly Mexican program. The Revolution failed to achieve most of Zapata's vision. Land reform remained incomplete. Indigenous populations remained marginalized. Yet it permanently altered the nation's trajectory. The Revolution's suppression of the Church, its emphasis on indigenous culture and mestizaje, racial mixture, and its assertion of economic sovereignty became permanent features of Mexican nationalism. It connects to Emilio Zapata, the southern peasant leader whose demand for land reform epitomized the Revolution's radical edge, to Pancho Villa, the northern general whose romantic legend made him the Revolution's most famous military figure, to Porfirio Díaz, the dictator whose fall triggered the Revolution and whose era the Revolution rejected, to the Constitution of nineteen seventeen, the revolutionary government's radical remaking of Mexico's legal order, to Diego Rivera, the muralist whose art became the visual language of revolutionary ideals, to the Cuban Revolution, the later Latin American revolution that the Mexican Revolution prefigured, to land reform, the central economic goal of the Revolution, to United States Mexico relations, the Revolution's assertion of sovereignty against United States intervention and corporate interests, to Indigenism, the celebration of indigenous culture that became central to post-revolutionary Mexican identity, and to Nationalism, the Revolution's assertion of Mexican control over Mexican resources and destiny.
